Organize all of the activations from one layer into a column as a vector.

What that means is that taking the weighted sum of the activations in the first layer according to these weights corresponds to one of the terms in the matrix vector product of everything we have on the left here.

lecture_notes: The lecture introduces a compact mathematical notation for neural network layer transitions using linear algebra. Instead of individual scalar operations, activations are organized into a column vector. Weights are structured into a matrix where each row represents connections to a specific neuron in the subsequent layer. The transition from one layer to the next is expressed as the matrix-vector product of the weights and activations, plus a bias vector. Finally, a sigmoid activation function is applied element-wise to the resulting vector. This approach simplifies the mathematical representation and improves computational efficiency by leveraging optimized matrix multiplication libraries.
key_points: Represent layer activations as a column vector.
Represent weights as a matrix where rows correspond to connections to a specific target neuron.
Express the layer transition as: sigmoid(WeightMatrix * ActivationVector + BiasVector).
Matrix notation significantly simplifies code implementation and enhances performance.
Machine learning performance relies heavily on efficient linear algebra operations.
inferred_knowledge: Neural network computations can be parallelized effectively due to the structure of matrix multiplication.
The complexity of neural network code is reduced by abstracting scalar operations into vector and matrix operations.
Standard machine learning libraries are optimized specifically for linear algebra operations to handle large-scale data.
